p.t: Run **paid ads only on products with a healthy margin** (the profit left after all costs). Thin-margin products stay in free listings.
Check the **MAP** (minimum advertised price, the lowest price a shop may show in ads) before you list a product.
Do not offer a **price-match guarantee** on products whose supplier does not enforce MAP.
When a competitor breaks MAP, **take screenshots**, send them to the supplier, and follow up.

**Each supplier has its own prices and rules.** Check them one supplier at a time.
Your wholesale cost should be **50% or less** of MAP, the lowest advertised price.

Count every cost first, including shipping, fees and ads. Then set the price.
**Shipping can erase your profit.** Check it before you list a product.

**Build steady sales first.** Then ask the supplier for better prices.
Run paid ads only on products whose profit covers the ad cost.
If a competitor sells below the MAP (the lowest price the brand allows you to advertise), **send the supplier screenshots** and ask them to fix it.

Set aside **a share of every sale** in its own account so you can pay supplier bills.
If the supplier does not fix a MAP violation, **stop paid ads** for that brand.

p.t: Cost of goods sold (COGS) is only accurate when it is entered per product in Shopify.
COGS equals the cost to deliver the product to your 3PL plus the average shipping cost per unit to the customer.

Packaging and supplies cover only the materials used to fulfil an order: the box, tape, polymailer and the cost of the shipping label itself. Postage paid to the carrier is entered separately as shipping cost.
Shipping cost is the average postage paid per order for a typical order size, for example $9.17. Take it from actual carrier costs, not from packaging.
If a 3PL charges per pick, an order with several items incurs one pick fee per item, so the 3PL cost per order must be scaled to the average number of picks.
Typical 3PL pick and pack fees run about $1.50 to $2.50 per pick. If no 3PL is used, this input is $0.
Keep COGS as low as possible, but never at the expense of the quality customers notice. Cutting costs that buyers feel will hurt repeat sales.

Customisation and rush production options from the supplier carry their own costs. Add a markup to them, and ask suppliers which custom or rush options they offer before building them into your pricing.
A supplier's percentage margin must be checked for its basis. Ask whether it is a net margin left after the product cost or a markup on that cost.

The two give very different selling prices, so confirm which one applies before committing.
**Worked cost examples**
Ceramic flower pot: sold at $30 (about $29.90) with an $11 COGS including fulfilment costs.
Zendrop: one unit sourced at $20 with $10 shipping to the customer gives a total of $30 entered as COGS + SHIPPING per unit.

CJ Dropshipping: a cost of $17 per item on CJ was entered into profit calculators to check margin.
**CJ Dropshipping price basis**
On CJ Dropshipping, after you choose the variant and the target country, the product page shows a field called total dropshipping price.

It already includes the product cost and shipping to the customer, so use it as the base cost for pricing instead of the item price alone.

p.t:
1. Estimate the product cost from AliExpress listicles by checking average prices.
2. Open a sourcing request at CJ Dropshipping to get accurate supplier prices.
3. Use the sourcing result as the real cost basis for pricing.

AliExpress prices are only estimates, because sellers without fulfilment can set any price. Use a sourcing request to confirm the cost.
**Shipping outside the MAP**

Shipping costs are typically not included in a supplier's MAP price, because shipping varies by destination. If a supplier does not explicitly state that shipping is included in its pricing, assume it is not.

Estimating shipping and margin:
1. Find the supplier's location and zip code on its website.
2. Note the product's size and weight.
3. Get a freight estimate from freightbroker.com between the supplier's zip code and two customer zip codes in the states you plan to sell in, for example one in Florida and one in California.

4. Average the two estimates to get a shipping cost.
5. Subtract wholesale cost and shipping from the selling price to see the margin left for ads and fees.
Some suppliers based in Japan charge an average of about $15 shipping per product, which can remove most of the margin on lower-priced items.
Add this shipping cost into the spread calculation before listing their products.
If a supplier adds tax to its wholesale prices, compare competitor prices with that tax included and recalculate the MAP-to-wholesale spread. Keep the products only if the spread still works.
Google Shopping is used for competitor price research: search your product names as a customer, then compare sellers' prices to your wholesale cost.
Use store averages, not the lowest prices.

Extremely low competitor prices are often a warning sign rather than a bargain. Stores selling with almost no margin often have poor customer service, late or missing shipments and short business lifespans.
Check company names, websites, reviews and ratings before treating their price as market price.

p.t: The sources give different thresholds. Each one applies in a different situation, so read them together.

**50% rule (core target)**
Value: Wholesale about half of MAP. A $1,000 MAP implies a $500 wholesale cost.
When it applies: Default test for every supplier.

**Target spread**
Value: Wholesale of $1,000 should correspond to a MAP of about $2,000.
When it applies: Planning target when reviewing a price list.

**Minimum multiple**
Value: MAP at least 2x wholesale.
When it applies: Floor after fees, acquisition, shipping and overhead.

**Ideal multiple**
Value: MAP at least 2.2x wholesale.
When it applies: Preferred level; thin spreads should be reconsidered.

**Formula shown by suppliers**
Value: A MAP formula such as 2x wholesale.
When it applies: When the supplier sheet has no MAP policy.

**Shipping-inclusive margin floor**
Value: At least 25% margin including shipping.
When it applies: Listing decision for a product.

**Average spread in one example**
Value: About 25%, against about 50% required by the model.
When it applies: Reference of what suppliers often offer.

**Typical retail discount offered**
Value: 15-20% off retail is below target.
When it applies: Spread check before paid ads.

**Floor before expenses**
Value: Never settle on a margin leaving about 20% before expenses.
When it applies: Hard floor during negotiation.

**Discount from supplier**
Value: 30% insufficient for an online retailer; 30-35% not enough if you also pay shipping and acquisition.

When it applies: Supplier discounts that still must cover shipping and ads.
**Discount from supplier**
Value: 50% acceptable; 20-40% usually not.

When it applies: Judged by whether COGS is about 50% of planned selling price.
**Affiliate-style margin**
Value: 10-20% before payment fees and ad costs.

When it applies: Sign of an affiliate-style relationship; not enough to build a business.
**Affiliate minimum**

Value: A minimum affiliate discount of 30% is not profitable; at 20%, decline or price above MAP without paid traffic.
When it applies: Affiliate offers.

**No-MAP starting price**
Value: Price around three times wholesale as a starting point.
Benchmarks: MAP, wholesale and the 50% rule (continued)

p.t:
When it applies: Only when no MAP is given; revise against margin math and competitor prices.
**No-MAP fallback**

Value: Set price at least 2x wholesale.
When it applies: When no clear competitor price can be found.
Where sources give different starting points for a supplier with no MAP, use the 3x starting point only as a first guess. Use the 2x fallback when no clear competitor price exists.

Revise both against competitor prices and your own margin.
Under the 50% rule, if a supplier's price is far off and it will not negotiate, the supplier is usually not worth working with.
The minimum acceptable wholesale margin is about 50%. A wholesale cost above half of MAP should be negotiated or reconsidered.
Judge a discount by the resulting cost of goods, not by the percentage alone. A 50% discount can be acceptable, while 20-40% off usually is not.
Off-MSRP example: a supplier offering 50% off MSRP while MAP is 25% off MSRP leaves too little margin. The deal only works if competitors sell at MSRP.
**Worked profit example at 2x**
Wholesale $800, sale price $1,000: gross profit $200. Minus 2.9% fees ($29) gives $171. Minus 10% customer acquisition cost ($100) gives $71 profit.
Subtracting shipping and operational overhead leaves minimal or negative margin.
Solution: price at $1,600 instead, and drive only organic and remarketing traffic, not paid ads.

Transaction fees (2.9%) and customer acquisition (up to 10% of sale) are the costs that a 2x MAP has to cover.
**Dollar profit matters as much as percentage**
A wholesale price of $161 against a MAP of $230 leaves too little dollar profit per sale to justify advertising.
Accepting a lower spread is only reasonable for very high-ticket products worth thousands of dollars, where gross profit per unit is still large.
A lower spread is acceptable only when the dollar profit per sale still makes the sale worthwhile.

p.t: Established industry suppliers offered about $125 profit on a $1,000 product and about $200 on a $4,000 product, which can be too thin for paid ads.
Do not sell products at very low margins, such as 5% or a flat $50 per sale. This is especially true for suppliers without a price policy, where other retailers race to the bottom.
These deals create more problems than sales.

Products sold below 25% margin including shipping should not be added to the store. Keep the supplier on file for later.
**Product-level margin checks**
Product-only margin in the example was roughly 20% once outbound shipping was removed, showing that shipping was the main reason the margin was low.
Outbound shipping in the example cost about $98,000 to $100,000 per year, roughly 6.3% of total income. It is one of the largest levers for improving margin.
Check each product's margin including shipping before listing it. Add only products with at least 25% margin including shipping.
Small, lightweight products have low fulfilment costs because they ship in small packages. This leaves room for a good selling price and margin, so use it when choosing test products.
Outbound shipping cost in one case was about $98,000 per year; the owner planned to bring it to about $75,000, a saving of about $23,000 per year, while keeping the rest of the cost structure.

This was the third of three supplier priorities.
**Margin review steps**
1. Contact the supplier and build the relationship before asking for terms.

2. Request the supplier's current pricing sheet.
3. Calculate the margin for each product, including shipping.
4. Add only products with at least 25 percent margin including shipping.
5. Keep low-margin suppliers on file and note any individual high-margin products they offer.
6. Keep searching for higher-margin suppliers as the first priority.
Products from suppliers with weak sales can stay listed in free Google Shopping listings if they still show margin, so they earn traffic without ad spend.

p.t: **Supplier margin is set per supplier**
Margins are supplier-specific, not niche-specific. No actual margin is known before approval, because pricing tiers and credit terms differ by supplier.
One supplier may offer 50% margin while another in the same niche offers only 25-30%.

The profit margin is set by each supplier, not by the niche. Two suppliers in the same niche can offer very different margins, so judge every supplier on its own price list before deciding what to sell.
Supplier margins are negotiated per supplier, not per niche. A low 20-30% margin from one supplier does not mean the niche is wrong. Keep adding approved suppliers in the niche.
Margin between MAP and wholesale varies by supplier, not by niche. Calculate each supplier's margin after approval rather than assuming an industry margin.
Supplier-specific prices, MAP policies and margins are unknown until approval. Use category averages for planning and confirm the real margins after approval.
Wholesale cost is not known until you are approved, but you can still plan around it.
A supplier's price list is the fastest way to confirm true profit per supplier. Margins can often only be confirmed after approval, but they can be calculated as soon as the price list is received.
Approved suppliers typically send an Excel sheet with three columns, or three separate price lists: MSRP, MAP and wholesale. Use these to estimate margins before listing products.

**Checking a supplier with no MAP policy**
1. Get the supplier's price list.
2. Search Google Shopping for several of its products.

3. Check whether anyone already advertises those products and at what markup.
4. If competitors mark them up only 10% or 15%, do not list them; this is a no-go.
5. If there is little competition, become the main seller for those products; if competitors sell them at healthy margins, list them too.

1. Search the supplier's products in Google Shopping.
2. Check the prices other sellers use for those products.
3. If sellers are selling at no margin, skip the supplier.

4. If sellers still make a healthy margin, sell the products and mark them as ineligible on your price match policy page.
1. Search the product names on Google Shopping.

2. Compare the prices other sellers charge.
3. Drop the product if many sellers price it at almost no margin, because that is a race to the bottom.

4. If margins hold up, exclude the product from your price match policy before the first sale.
1. Search for that brand on Google Shopping.

3. If competitors are listing at very low markup (e.g., 5% margin), list the product on your site but only target free/organic traffic (no paid ads).
4. If competitors have healthy markups, you can list at similar prices and use Google Shopping ads.

When no MAP policy exists, check the supplier's price list, shipping estimate and competitor prices before listing its products.
Compare the expected margin for each brand before committing, since margins can still be strong when the brand approves only selected retailers.
Brands that approve retailers selectively, especially those without a MAP policy, can still offer good margins because other retailers also protect their prices.
Do not undercut the best competitor price in these cases, because price wars leave no one profitable.
Pricing for a brand with no MAP starts from competitor prices. If competitors sell above your planned price, match their price instead of undercutting them, since buyers pay more.

1. Search Google for a few products of that brand as a normal customer would.
2. Open Google Shopping and check what competitors list the same products for.
3. If competitors sell above your planned price, match their price instead of undercutting them, since buyers pay more.
4. If you cannot find a clear competitor price, set the price at least 2x wholesale.
If competitors sell a popular product at only about 1.5x wholesale, you can still list it at 2x wholesale but run no paid ads for it.
Let it earn sales from free Google product listings and SEO instead of spending money where you cannot beat the price.
**Judging a supplier's position and terms**
Suppliers that sell direct at MSRP and let retailers sell at MAP are good partners. Avoid brands that sell at MAP themselves or below MAP, because this removes your price advantage.

p.t: If a brand sells direct at MAP, look for a unique value proposition (UVP), such as better presentation, trust or customer experience, that sets your store apart.
Skip the brand if its own site already sells well and it expects you to match or beat its price.
Retail margins are usually the same for every reseller, so negotiate only if the numbers do not work.
Supplier prices are usually fixed once you are approved, so negotiation is rarely possible. Focus on the research and the approval process instead.
Some manufacturers sell direct at MSRP but allow retailers to sell at MAP, so a retailer can price below MSRP. Get approved, request the price list and confirm the margin before deciding.
When a brand is only available through a wholesaler, check the margin after the wholesaler's price and whether you have pricing control.
Working through the wholesaler is acceptable when margin and pricing are right.
A supplier that sells the same product direct at the same price with free shipping leaves no room for a value proposition.
List such products only if the store offers a bonus or better service; otherwise skip the supplier. (Older advice? Undated, 2023.)
If a supplier sells direct to consumers and runs its own paid ads, listing its products on your store can still help build credibility when approaching other brands.
Do not include them in paid ads, since they are unlikely to become a major earner. (2025.)
If the supplier also sells directly to consumers at MAP, check its own retail website before deciding: whether it runs ads and whether the site is built to convert visitors.
A supplier that does not invest in its retail channel can still be a profitable partner.

Judge a supplier's offer on its own numbers before listing. Approval does not mean every product is worth selling.
**Supplier with thin margin after shipping**
If a supplier's margin is too thin after shipping, drop that supplier's products even after approval. Approval does not mean every product is worth selling.

Supplier margins of 10-20% before payment fees and ad costs signal an affiliate-style relationship. Negotiate with these suppliers or skip them in favour of suppliers that meet the 50% wholesale rule.
Negotiating better terms
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: **Timing: when negotiation works**
In the early stage, with minimal sales history, you have little negotiating power with suppliers for better rates or terms. Focus optimisation on conversions and product selection.
Negotiate more heavily once you have proven sales volume.
Wholesale cost is usually not negotiable for a brand-new retailer, even one with a track record in other businesses. Suppliers typically want proof of sales first.
Wholesale cost becomes negotiable as your sales volume with that supplier grows.
Once a relationship is established, a supplier may give about 10% off wholesale cost. Some suppliers also offer special holiday pricing so the retailer can sell more of their products.
Demand comes before cost. Build consistent demand first, for example 20 sales per day consistently and later 50 per day. Inconsistent demand is a bigger problem than supplier cost at an early stage.

Validate first, then negotiate once you know the product will scale. Keep a second backup supplier so you can justify the price.
**Basic sourcing sequence**
1. Start with CJ Dropshipping for convenience, since it is easy to set up and offers acceptable prices and shipping.
2. Build consistent demand first, for example 20 sales per day consistently and later 50 per day.
3. Once demand is steady, contact other suppliers, state your sales volume and ask whether they can beat your current price.

4. Move the business only if the new supplier matches or beats the price and service.
**Negotiation procedures**

1. Ask your current supplier, such as CJ, whether they can lower the price.
2. Request quotes from several other suppliers for the same product.
3. Compare the quotes and choose the supplier that gives the best margin and delivery terms.
In the shoe example, fulfilment cost per pair was about $13 to $15 after negotiation. That cost still left a healthy margin on a selling price of $40.
A jewelry product with a fulfilment cost of about $7 per item allowed a selling price of $30 with a comfortable margin. The margin came from low cost of goods rather than from a high selling price.
Check your supplier's best price rather than accepting the first offer, and ask whether the price can go lower once you have scale.

**Negotiation procedure with a volume threshold**
1. Obtain the supplier's price list showing wholesale and MAP.

p.t: 2. If MAP is not about double the wholesale price, state that the price must be at that level to sell and that otherwise the brand will not be sold.
3. Ask immediately whether the supplier offers volume-based pricing incentives, for example a discount once a monthly dollar or unit threshold is reached.

4. Track monthly volume and follow up for the discount once the threshold is reached.
**Incentive pricing after approval**
1. Once you are approved, get their price list and upload their products right away.
2. Ask whether they offer incentive pricing for selling a set number of units per month or for reaching revenue targets.
3. Ask whether they give discounts off wholesale prices for your account.
4. Before the busy season (Black Friday, Cyber Monday through Christmas), contact them again to negotiate special seasonal pricing.
Template: incentive pricing request
Hi [Supplier contact name], we are now approved and have uploaded your products to our store at [store domain].
Do you offer any incentive pricing if we sell [number] units per month or reach [revenue target] in revenue?
Are there any discounts off wholesale prices that would be available to us, and do you offer special pricing during busy periods such as Black Friday, Cyber Monday and the holiday season?

Thank you, [Your name].
**Requesting better margins**
Ask suppliers for a tiered retailer discount structure early in the process. Standard options include a percentage off wholesale or discounts at set sales volumes.
Ask whether the supplier offers tiered retailer pricing, such as 20% off wholesale. Ask for discounts at set sales volumes, such as a number of units or sales.
Decide to list or advertise the products only after you see the final margins.
A supplier can be asked for better margins with a specific framing: say you want to promote their products and spend more on ads, and ask about incentive pricing.
Start with friendly questions rather than an immediate request for discounts.

Before running ads on a supplier offering a 15-20% discount off retail, ask for better margins first. Some stores have negotiated better margins with suppliers, so a low spread can sometimes be improved.

p.t: When a supplier adds a drop-ship fee, shipping and taxes that erode your margin, negotiate first. If prices cannot change, exclude that supplier from paid ads, because organic sales still earn margin.
Remove the supplier if the margin is still too small.
Ask whether a supplier offers a value-for-volume deal.
Ask for better wholesale prices, incentive or volume programmes, and whether a retailer hitting a set number of units or sales unlocks lower wholesale prices.
Add the question to your early calls: ask suppliers for their tiered retailer discount structure, including volume discounts. Ask for 5 or 10 percent off at set sales levels.
Template: asking for better margins
Hi, this is [Your name] from [Store name]. Now that we have reviewed your price sheets, we want to move a good number of your products.
After running the numbers, our margins are lower than we expected, around [current margin]%, and we need closer to [target margin]% to run ads profitably.
Do you have other pricing tiers, or is there room to negotiate better margins for us?
We would also like product photos and videos we are allowed to use, and we would like to order one sample unit at wholesale price to inspect the quality before we commit.
Template: volume-based discount request
Hi [Supplier name], we have been ordering from you since [month and year] and placed about [total annual order value] in orders over the last twelve months, so we are one of your larger accounts.
We would like to discuss better pricing for next year. Could you offer us [5] percent or [10] percent lower prices on [product list or category], and could you send your volume pricing tiers?
If we can agree on this, we can commit to about [expected monthly order volume] orders. Thank you, [Your name], [Company name].

Hi, this is [your name] from [your brand]. We were looking over the price lists you sent us.
We really want to put a real ad budget behind these products and become one of your top retailers, but the margins aren't where we need them to be.
Do you have any incentive programs where, if retailers reach a certain number of units or a certain sales volume, wholesale prices get discounted?

p.t:
If not, please let me know so we can decide our next steps.
Ask a supplier whether a discount is allowed:

1. Collect screenshots of competitor coupons or discount pop-ups.
2. Email the sales rep with the screenshots and ask whether you may do the same.

3. If there is no reply, follow up briefly to make sure the email was seen.
**Excess stock and special offers**
Suppliers often hold excess or discontinued stock they want to clear quickly, and offer discounts of up to 40% for sellers who promote it.
A store that already has traffic can start moving that stock almost immediately by featuring the products or running new ads on them.
A brick-and-mortar retailer must place a bulk order, wait for shelf space and then handle the stock before it can sell.

When a service provider such as a finisher or waterproofing shop has to market its services itself, you can ask for a discount if you can line up a steady group of customers who need the same service.

The provider accepts a lower price because you reduce its acquisition effort and time.
**Using the list of suppliers as leverage**
When competitors sell the same product for less than your supplier price list allows, they most likely have better supplier pricing or better shipping rates. They are not usually selling at a loss.
Ask suppliers about the product's price when a competitor is undercutting you. Possible answers include a cheaper carrier or a lower wholesale tier.
Email the supplier with your wholesale price, the competitor's price with free shipping and your shipping cost. Ask whether they can offer better pricing or cheaper shipping.
Template: wholesale and shipping pressure
Hi [rep name], This is the wholesale price you gave me for [product]: [wholesale price]. A competitor is selling it for [competitor price] with free shipping.

My shipping cost for this item would be about [shipping cost], which leaves me no profit. Is there any way we could get better pricing or a cheaper shipping option? Thank you for your help. [your name]
Shipping costs in one case reached 30-50% of product cost for distributor shipping, and the most popular supplier's products shipped at about 40%.
The recommended path was to show the supplier real figures (sales count, shipments, shipping costs and remaining margin) and request preferred-carrier shipping or incentive pricing,
then compare freight broker quotes. Raising prices above MAP, adding a large shipping fee or dropping the brand were rejected, because sales would fall and ad spend would be wasted.
Low-margin handling
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t:
**Options when the spread is too thin**
The spread is the gap between what you pay and what you sell for.
1. **Contact** the supplier to negotiate better wholesale pricing (the price the supplier charges you, before your markup).
2. If the margin is still acceptable but ad spend is unaffordable, **keep** the product and rely on organic traffic only (visitors who find you without paid ads).

3. Otherwise, **drop** the product.
Low-margin products can still be listed without paid campaigns (ads you pay for).
Keep them in **free Google product listings** (free product entries in Google Shopping, Google's price comparison page) for organic traffic.
Keep paid campaigns focused on products with the **largest spread**.
If a supplier's margin is too thin, **either do not list** its products or list them without any paid ads, so only free traffic reaches them.
Products with too small a margin to advertise can still be listed on the store and in the free listings section of Google Shopping, with **no ad budget**.

Spend paid traffic only on products from suppliers with **healthy margins**.
Send the full catalogue to free Google product listings.
Add suppliers to paid campaigns only after their margins are **proven**.
Non-MAP suppliers (suppliers that do not set a MAP): **do not run** Google Shopping ads for products where competitors undercut your price on every listing (sell cheaper than you).

Invest in free traffic sources instead.
Do not expose the products to price-match guarantees.
When margins are too thin, **ask** suppliers whether they have incentive or volume programmes (discounts for reaching a set number of units or sales) that lower wholesale prices.

If the answer is no, decide whether to list the brand with **no ad spend** or skip it entirely.
**Do not match** prices of non-MAP competitors when no margin is available.
Low-margin handling (continued)
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: If the supplier enforces MAP, **ask it to contact** the competitor.
Otherwise keep your price where you can make money, and do not run Google Shopping ads on those products.
**Do not sell** a product at a price below MAP through advertising.
If a supplier that does not enforce MAP sells the same product elsewhere, **check** it has no price-match policy before approaching.

If margins are too thin, exclude those products from paid ads and rely on free Google Shopping listings.
**Thin margin: a shipping example**
1. **Calculate the margin:** retail price minus wholesale cost minus shipping. Example: $699 - $530 = $169, but $200 shipping would leave a loss.
2. **Email the supplier** with your wholesale price, the competitor's price with free shipping and your shipping cost. Ask whether they can offer better pricing or cheaper shipping.
3. If the supplier refuses, still list the product if people search for it, but **exclude it** from paid traffic.
4. **Price the product** with your own margin, and exclude it from your price-match guarantee.
5. **Add perceived value** (how valuable the customer feels the offer is) with bonuses and shipping upgrades, such as white-glove delivery (premium delivery with setup).
A supplier's cost should be **checked against its MAP** before it is listed.
A thin spread should be reconsidered or negotiated (see the 2x and 50% benchmarks above).
If a supplier adds a drop-ship fee (an extra charge for shipping from the supplier) or tax that erodes (reduces) margin, **first negotiate**.

If prices cannot change, keep the product on free traffic only.
**Do not sell** at very low margins.
**Do not advertise** products whose spread has become too thin.
Ad versus free-traffic decisions

p.t: **Paid versus free listing by margin**

Spend paid traffic only on products from suppliers with **healthy margins**.
Send the full catalogue to free Google product listings.

Keep the paid campaigns focused on products with the **largest spread**.
Products with thin spreads stay in free listings.
Products from suppliers with weak sales can remain in free Google Shopping listings if they still show margin, so they earn traffic **without ad spend**.

Keep products with thin margins in **free listings only**, so that organic traffic can still reach them.
**Checking whether a supplier's product is working**
When a supplier's products get **more than 100 unique visitors** (different people, each counted once) from paid ads without any sale, shoppers are most likely buying from the supplier directly.
**Check unique visitors per supplier product** before deciding whether to keep advertising it. (2023.)
If big retailers ignore a supplier's MAP enforcement, **check that supplier's SKUs** (stock codes, one per product version) one by one.

Advertise only products where big retailers are **not selling at a lower price**.
Filtering this way keeps ad spend on products you can actually sell at MAP. (2023.)

**Products that do not sell**
1. First **optimise** (improve) the product pages and the ads for those products.
2. If they still do not sell, **lower the target cost per click** (the most you pay for one click) for them in Google Shopping, so they still show but receive less budget.
3. If that fails, **remove** them from your paid alpha and beta campaigns (paid ad campaigns with those names), and let them sell through free Google product listings and organic search.

**Competitor price-cutting in paid campaigns**
1. **Take screenshots** of the violating listings and send them to your supplier.
2. Watch how the supplier responds. A supplier that acts quickly is the first step.
Ad versus free-traffic decisions (continued)

p.t: 3. If the supplier is not helpful, **check how your ads convert** (turn visitors into sales) for those specific products.
If they do not convert and the spend looks like unfair competition, **drastically lower the bids** (the amount you offer per click) for those products,
rather than removing them from the feed (the product list you send to Google). (2023.)

**Stop** paid ads for a supplier's products when the supplier's margin does not hold after shipping and ad costs.
Keep the products on the store for organic traffic.
**Ad spend after a supplier discount**
A supplier discount of **30-35%** is not enough if you still pay shipping and must fund customer acquisition (the cost of winning each new buyer).

Ask suppliers for better margins, check whether they offer pricing tiers (price levels by order size), and review their terms, exclusivity (whether only you may sell the product) and pricing before deciding
which products to fund with paid traffic. (2025.)
Products where a **2x MAP** (the price is twice the wholesale cost) leaves room are run in ads only if the remaining profit covers acquisition.

A 2x MAP at 10% customer acquisition still needs the rest of the costs covered.
**Ad decision by supplier type**

Suppliers that sell direct to consumers and undercut your price while running ads are hard to beat.
Keep them on the store **without ads** and rely on organic traffic.
Advertise products where your store adds value. (2023.)
For a product where competitors undercut your price, **bid lower and run no ads** on those products instead of matching their price.
Direct-to-consumer undercutting
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: Direct-to-consumer means the brand sells straight to shoppers, not only through shops.
A brand selling direct to consumers is a good partner when it sells at **MSRP** (manufacturer's suggested retail price) and lets retailers sell at MAP.
Avoid brands that sell at MAP themselves or **below MAP**, because this removes your price advantage.
If a brand sells direct at MAP, **look for a unique value proposition** (a reason customers should buy from you, such as better presentation, trust or customer experience).
Skip the brand if its own site already sells well and it expects you to match or beat its price.
If a supplier sells direct to consumers at the same price and advertises in the same channels as you, **stop paid ads** to its product pages.
Keep those products only in free Google Shopping listings, where organic traffic can still arrive. (2023.)

Once an approved supplier is strong direct-to-consumer, keep it on your store but **stop spending** on it:
1. **Remove** its products from the Google Shopping product feed.

2. Keep the products live for organic traffic.
3. Put ad budget into products from suppliers you have not yet onboarded (brought onto your store).

(2023.)
Suppliers that sell direct to consumers and undercut your price while running ads are hard to beat.

Keep them on the store **without ads** and rely on organic traffic.
Advertise products where your store adds value. (2023.)
A supplier that sells the same product direct at the same price with **free shipping** does not leave the store room for a value proposition. (2023.)

If a supplier sells direct and runs its own paid ads, **do not include** its products in your paid ads.
Listing them can still add credibility. (2025.)

**Do not match** prices of non-MAP competitors when no margin is available.
If the supplier enforces MAP, **ask it to contact** the competitor. (2021.)
Price-match guarantees, coupons and advertised price
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: A price-match guarantee is a promise to match a lower price.
A coupon code is a discount code entered at checkout (the last payment step).
Coupon codes that reduce price **below MAP** are generally acceptable, because MAP is the minimum advertised price, not the minimum selling price.

Check individual supplier agreements for language forbidding promotional codes.
The advertised price (the price shown in ads and emails) **must not go below MAP**.
A coupon code applied at checkout can lower the price the customer pays, because the advertised price stays at MAP.
Product-specific discounts that only apply at checkout are generally allowed unless a supplier forbids them. (2023.)
Clear coupon mechanisms that only apply at checkout are the **only standard exception** to not selling below MAP through advertising.
MAP is a minimum advertised price, so you may advertise a product **above** it but not below it.

A retailer below MAP is in violation of the supplier's policy. (2025.)
**Ask whether the supplier has a MAP policy** after approval.
If it does not, the site should **not carry a price guarantee**, because it can only be honoured when MAP applies.
**Do not offer** a price-match guarantee on a supplier's product pages if that supplier does not enforce MAP.
Otherwise a competitor willing to sell at a loss can force you to match and lose money on every sale.
**Do not work through** a supplier's MAP with a price-match guarantee if the supplier does not use MAP.
A price guarantee promises to match a lower price from an authorised retailer (a shop the brand approves), which only fits MAP-enforced products.

Products from non-MAP suppliers **do not require** price-match policies. (2025.)
Before approaching a non-MAP supplier, **confirm** that it has no price-match policy.
Template: asking whether a supplier has a MAP policy
Hi [Supplier name], I wanted to ask whether you have a MAP policy. I searched [product name] on Google Shopping and found it listed at [price 1], [price 2] and [price 3] (screenshots attached).
Could you let me know how you see this pricing?
MAP violations: detection, reporting and enforcement
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: A MAP violation means a seller advertises a price below the brand's minimum.

**Confirm and document the violation**
**Take a screenshot** of every case where a competitor breaks the MAP policy, including sales on Amazon.
Send the screenshots to your supplier's sales rep (the supplier's sales contact).
Expect a **quick fix** if the supplier enforces the policy; a slow response shows how strictly it is enforced.

**Take a screenshot** of the competitor's product page showing the price that violates MAP.
Confirm the price is **live on several devices**. (2025.)
To report a competitor selling a MAP product below the minimum advertised price, **take a screenshot** of the lower price. (2025.)
When a competitor sells below MAP and your ads face unfair price competition, **take screenshots** of the violating listings and send them to your supplier. (2023.)

**Take screenshots** of the below-MAP listing before contacting the supplier. (2026.)
**Report to the supplier**
Procedure:

1. **Contact** your supplier representative.
2. **Send screenshots** of the violation.
3. **See whether** the supplier takes action.

4. **Do not match** the competitor's price yourself.
Procedure:
1. **Capture a screenshot** of the competitor's product page showing the price that violates MAP, and confirm the price is live on several devices.
2. **Email the brand's contact person** with the competitor's URL, the MAP price, the listed price and the screenshot, and ask them to address it.
3. The brand typically contacts the retailer and gives a **deadline** to correct the price.

4. If the retailer does not comply, the brand can **remove the retailer's permission** to sell its products. (2025.)
Procedure (Source A, report):

1. **Take a screenshot** of the competitor's product page showing the lower price.
2. **Email your contact at the brand** with the screenshot.
3. State the listed price and the MAP, and ask whether the MAP policy has changed. Do not demand that the competitor be banned.
MAP violations: detection, reporting and enforcement (continued)
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: 4. The brand contacts the violating store and usually gives it a **set number of days** to correct the price.

5. A store that violates MAP repeatedly can **lose the right** to sell that brand's products. (2025.)
Procedure (Source A, Amazon sale):

1. **Ask the supplier** whether the lower price is its new price and whether you may sell at that price.
2. If the supplier says yes, **change your price** to match.
3. If the supplier refuses to follow its own MAP policy, **remove that supplier's products** from your Google Shopping feed so you do not pay for traffic on them.

Procedure (Source A, marketplace below MAP):
1. **Capture screenshots** of the marketplace prices (large online sales sites such as Amazon).
2. **Email your supplier representative** as soon as possible.
3. Ask whether the MAP policy changed, whether the supplier permits this pricing, and whether you may sell at that price.

4. **Decide your next step** based on the reply. (2024.)
Procedure (Source A, below-MAP listing):
1. **Take screenshots** of the below-MAP listing.

2. **Email the supplier** with the screenshots and ask whether they are aware the product is listed at that price. (2026.)
Procedure (Walmart, 2022):
If competitors on Walmart.com are selling a product below MAP, **contact your supplier** with screenshot links showing the violation.

Ask them to enforce MAP with third-party sellers (sellers who are not the brand). Most suppliers will take action.
**Check a supplier's response**
Procedure:

1. **Take a screenshot** of every case where a competitor breaks the MAP policy, including sales on Amazon.
2. **Send the screenshots** to your supplier's sales rep.
3. **Expect a quick fix** if the supplier enforces the policy; a slow response shows how strictly it is enforced.
When a competitor violates MAP, **follow up repeatedly** with your brand rep (your brand contact) instead of reporting once and waiting.
MAP agreements bind every authorised seller, so the brand has a responsibility to enforce them.

A supplier that does not act on **constant MAP violations** is a bad sign.
Serious suppliers take listings down quickly when violations are reported.
MAP violations: detection, reporting and enforcement (continued)
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: When a supplier does not enforce MAP, **decide** whether to keep paying to advertise those products or to keep them out of the paid budget. (2023.)
When a third-party seller on a large marketplace sells a supplier's product below MAP, **report it** to the supplier, since this has led to price changes. (2023.)

If a supplier does not respond about a MAP violation, **follow up after a few days**, especially after a holiday weekend.
Procedure (Source A, no reply):

1. **Follow up** after a few days, especially after a holiday weekend.
2. **Restate** that the violation is still happening.

3. If there is still no reply, **stop running ads** for that supplier's products.
4. **Remove** those products from the store if the violation continues.

A supplier whose MAP is violated by big-box stores (large chain shops) selling below the wholesale price must **fix the violation** before the store lists the product at a higher price in paid channels. (2024.)
**Report MAP violators** that list products far below MAP to Google so that their listings are removed.
Prices at **half of MAP or less** are a sign of a scam (a trick to take money) or fraud, not a sustainable business model. (2024.)
A supplier that offered a better discount for a long time may drop its terms.
Use your historical sales and margin data per product (your past records) to decide which items keep ad budget, and **remove the rest** from the paid feed. (2024.)
Some supplier discounts can change over time.
**Keep the supplier's price sheet (its list of prices and terms) under review, and re-check margins** before continuing ads. (2024.)

Procedure (Source A, supplier's MAP not reaching 2x):
1. **Ask for better wholesale pricing.**

2. Ask whether they offer tiered retailer pricing, such as **20% off** wholesale.
3. Ask for discounts at set sales volumes, such as a number of units or sales.

4. **Decide to list or advertise** the products only after you see the final margins. (2023.)
**Supplier with no MAP policy: asking about MAP**

After approval, **ask each supplier** whether it has a minimum advertised price (MAP) policy.
If it does not, the site should **not carry a price guarantee**.
MAP violations: detection, reporting and enforcement (continued)
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: If the supplier does not provide a MAP policy in its sheet, it may state a formula such as **2x wholesale**.
You can also search the product name and compare competitor listings to see the actual advertised price. (2023.)
A Google Shopping search of a supplier's products shows whether sellers price below MAP.

**Search a sample** of the supplier's products every few items, record violations in the supplier's notes, and switch to scheduled audits (regular planned checks) once the supplier is confirmed to enforce

MAP.
Procedure (Source A, enforcement failure):
1. **Check** whether your own sales happen at MAP and whether traffic is profitable.

2. If yes, **continue**.
3. If not, **remove the supplier's products from the alpha and beta campaigns and stop paying** for their traffic.

4. **Keep letting free traffic** reach those products.
Procedure (Source A, supplier with no MAP):
1. **Search** the supplier's products in Google Shopping.

2. **Check the prices** other sellers use for those products.
3. If sellers are selling at no margin, **skip the supplier**.

4. If sellers still make a healthy margin, **sell the products** and mark them as ineligible on your price match policy page.
Procedure (Source A, ask about MAP with a request):

1. **Ask the supplier** whether it has a MAP policy.
2. **Show the search results** you found on Google Shopping, with screenshots, and ask how it sees the pricing.
Template: MAP inquiry to supplier (2021)
Hi [supplier contact name], I found [competitor name] selling [product name] at [price], which appears to be below your MAP (screenshot attached).
Could you tell me what the MAP is for this product, and why this company is not selling at it? Thank you, [your name]
If a supplier's MAP does not make it into the sheet, **use competitor listings and the supplier's stated formula** as the reference. (2023.)
If a supplier does not enforce MAP, and its products are sold at or below MAP in the same channels, **check the margin** before advertising.
Competitor pricing for non-MAP products
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: For non-MAP supplier products, **search for that brand** on Google Shopping and check what prices competitors list the

products at. (2025.)
**Judge a supplier** by its own price list before listing products.
Two suppliers in one niche can offer different margins.
If competitors mark a product up only 10% or 15%, **do not list it**. This is a no-go.
Non-MAP supplier products: list the product on your site with free traffic only if competitors list at very low markup, **around 5% margin**. (2025.)
Non-MAP suppliers: **do not advertise** where competitors undercut your price on every listing. (2022.)
Use this order when a new supplier is added. A supplier is the company that ships the products for you.
1. **Get the price list** from the approved supplier and upload its products.
2. **Confirm** whether a MAP policy exists. MAP (Minimum Advertised Price) is the lowest price the brand lets you advertise.
Also confirm whether the supplier enforces it, meaning it checks that sellers follow it.
3. **Calculate the margin** for each product. Margin is the money you keep from each sale. Include shipping, packaging, 3PL pick fees and payment fees.
A 3PL is an outside warehouse that packs and ships orders for you. A pick fee is the charge per order for that work. Payment fees are the charges for taking card payments.
4. **Compare** the spread against the 50% rule and the 2x floor. The spread is the gap between MAP and the wholesale cost, which is the price you pay the supplier.
The 2x floor means the price should be at least twice the wholesale cost.
5. **Decide** for each product: paid, free-only or dropped. "Paid" means you run paid ads for it.
"Free-only" means you list it with no ads and rely on organic traffic, which is free visitors from search and social media. "Dropped" means you remove it.
6. **Ask** for better margins, incentive pricing and volume tiers. Incentive pricing is a special lower price from the supplier. Volume tiers are prices that drop as you buy more.
7. **Renegotiate** once your sales volume is proven.
Priorities and sequencing
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: In the early stage, **focus** on conversions and product selection. A conversion is a visitor who buys.
Negotiating with suppliers gets easier once you have proven sales volume.
**Build steady demand** before you chase cost savings. Once steady sales are proven, negotiate supplier prices.
Keep a **backup supplier** so you can justify the price. Switch only when the new supplier matches or beats price and service.
Checks before listing a product
Pricing rules, margins and MAP requirements belong to each supplier. They do not belong to the niche.

A niche is a specific market you sell into.
**One low-margin supplier does not rule out** a niche. This is true if other suppliers offer the 50%-of-MAP structure.
Margins are set per supplier. They can differ within one store. Some suppliers offer 15%, others 20% or 30%. So **track margin per supplier**, not one store-wide figure.
Individual products from one supplier can also have different margins.
MAP requirements differ from brand to brand. **Run the 2x wholesale check** for each supplier, not once across the catalog. The catalog is your full product list.
If a brand's MAP is too close to its wholesale cost, **negotiate better pricing** before listing its products.
**Ask for the MAP policy** before you discount. Many suppliers allow discounts, but some forbid coupon codes.
p.h: Check the pricing rules before discounting

p.t: An automatic coupon can break the policy if it pushes the advertised price below MAP.
Extra discounts or coupon codes on top of MAP are allowed. The exception is when the supplier's retailer approval agreement forbids them. That is the contract a brand uses to approve sellers.
This restriction is rare. If a supplier has it, **exclude that brand** from promotions.
To find a brand's MAP without asking, **search the brand name on Google Shopping**. Google Shopping is Google's price comparison page. Compare the prices sellers list for its products.
Ask the supplier directly only if this does not reveal the price.
If a supplier's listed online price is below its MAP, **ask the supplier about it immediately**. Do not assume MAP is being enforced.
The 50% rule (wholesale against MAP)
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: Wholesale cost should be **no more than 50% of MAP**.
Example: a MAP of 5,000 USD requires a wholesale cost of 2,500 USD or less.

The spread must cover shipping, payment fees, ad spend and profit. Ad spend is what you pay for ads.
A wider spread leaves more room for these costs.

Exceptions are rare. They are only considered for **very expensive items** that sell consistently and easily.
MAP is often around **2x** the wholesale cost.
Margin calculations
Target a gross margin of about **25% to 30%** of the selling price. Gross margin is what is left after the product cost.
p.h: Build the full cost before committing

p.t:
Free shipping, the roughly 2.9% credit card fee and the ad cost to get each customer all come out of that margin.
**Build a full cost breakdown** before committing to a product.
When researching, use the AliExpress product price plus shipping to your country as the starting COGS. AliExpress is a large online marketplace.
COGS means cost of goods sold, which is what the product costs you. (2026)
**Recalculate** once you get real quotes from suppliers or fulfillment companies. Fulfillment companies pack and ship orders. Their quotes can be cheaper than AliExpress. (2026)
**Test** the sourcing and shipping cost of a product through CJ or the supplier before you launch ads. CJ is CJ Dropshipping, a supplier platform.

This matters most for large or heavy packages, where shipping can eat the margin.
Before pricing, **ask the supplier** for the product cost that applies to USA shipping. (2026)
Do not reuse a cost from another market. (2026)
The cost must cover the single unit. For bundles, it must cover the total cost for each quantity. A bundle is several items sold together. (2026)
**Calculate the landed cost**, including shipping, before choosing a heavy book for testing. Landed cost is the full cost to get the product to you. (2026)
Build the full cost before committing (continued)
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: Thick, heavy books have high cost of goods. Shipping to the US on the fast or slow shipping line adds a large cost on top. (2026)
Before calculating margin on a heavy product, **confirm** whether the supplier ships directly to the end customer.
Also confirm what shipping costs for that destination. Shipping cost often decides whether a niche is viable, more than the product cost does.
**Confirm** whether a supplier's price list applies per unit, per pack or per box before you publish a price.
A price list for two units sold as one item led a store to sell four units at **about half the intended price**.

Two units were delivered in one box. The supplier's price list showed the price for the two units together, not per unit.
The store sold four units at **about half the intended price**.
The store later considered asking the supplier to work on the price afterward, instead of accepting zero profit.
**Compare the sourcing price** with comparable Amazon prices before committing to a product. Amazon is a large online marketplace.
Example: a vacuum sealer device listed at $60-80 on AliExpress was judged too expensive for what it does. Meanwhile, a vacuum canister sold for $20-40 on Amazon.
Formula:
Profit after product cost = MAP − wholesale cost − average shipping cost − payment fees (2.9% for Shopify Payments) − other fees
Shopify Payments is Shopify's built-in payment service. "Other fees" means any extra costs not listed.

Example: MAP $1,000, wholesale $650 and shipping $100 leave **$250 before fees**.
In that example, roughly $210 is left after the fees. That number may be lower.
Arithmetic check: 2.9% of $1,000 is $29. That alone would leave about $221 from $250.

The source's roughly $210 implies further fees that it does not name.
Use the full cost list in and **recalculate per product**.
Estimate COGS for bookkeeping
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: Estimate COGS as **100% minus your gross margin**. For example, a 20% margin gives 80% COGS.

Base the estimate on the last six months of your P&L, which is your profit and loss statement.
Add a small buffer, meaning extra money set aside, so the COGS account never runs dry.
The result is an estimate. It is close enough to pay suppliers without checking each invoice to the cent.
The sources give different multiples. A multiple is a number you multiply a cost by.
They apply to different bases and situations, so check which one your store uses. Non-MAP means the supplier sets no MAP, so you choose the price yourself.

**Markup on landed cost**
Multiple: Selling price at least 3x landed cost (product plus shipping, COGS). Example: if landed cost is $10, sell for at least $30.

Source and year: Source C
When it applies: Needed to cover the average cost per purchase from TikTok ads. Below this margin it becomes very hard to be profitable.

**Product margin before ads**
Multiple: Product margin of at least 3x, calculated before running ads
Source and year: Source C

When it applies: Thin margins are a common reason beginners lose money despite sales.
**Non-MAP starting price**
Multiple: About 2.1x wholesale cost

Source and year: Source A
When it applies: Starting point for non-MAP suppliers, then compare with competitor prices on Google Shopping
**Non-MAP minimum**

Multiple: 2x wholesale cost
Source and year: Source A (undated) and 2021
When it applies: Minimum sale price for suppliers without MAP. Go higher if competitors sell above that level.

The 3x markup in means a sale price of three times landed cost. That is a gross margin of about 67% of the selling price.
That is well above the 25% to 30% gross margin target in.

The sources describe different measures. **Check the base** before applying a rule.
The source describes as a product margin of at least 3x. It does not define the base.

Read it alongside, which defines the base as landed cost.
Competitors may sell at **3 times MAP**. If so, a higher price than the 2.1x starting point is the right choice.
Net profit targets
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: Target a **net profit of 30 percent** per sale. Never go below 20 percent.
Accept 20 percent only for competitive products that need heavy ad spend, or for large bulk orders. Bulk means buying or selling in large amounts.
Reseller deals (deals where you buy to resell) should leave at least **20% net profit** after all costs. That is the minimum.

The actual deal needs a larger margin than that. Ads and credit card processing fees come out of it.
Formula for net profit per sale:
Net profit per sale = MAP − wholesale − shipping − ad spend per sale
Example with round numbers: 1,000 USD minus 500 USD wholesale, 100 USD free shipping and 100 USD ad spend leaves **300 USD net**.

That equals a 30 percent net margin.
This is not the same as the markup over wholesale. Markup is the extra on top of your cost.

Use the gross margin target for early screening, before shipping, fees and ads.
Use the net profit target for the **decision on each sale**.
The sources give these as different measures. They do not explain how the two fit together.
Shipping in the margin
Judge shipping cost against the product's **sale price and average order value**.
Average order value is the average amount a customer spends per order.
Do not judge shipping by weight alone. An $800 shipping cost on a $5,000 product can still leave about $1,500 net profit.
The same $800 on a $1,200 product destroys the margin.
Example: two dining tables of the same size and weight cost **$300** on average to ship. At $500 retail, the $300 shipping makes the product unworkable.
Judge shipping against price (continued)
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t:
At $1,500 retail, the same shipping cost is absorbable.
Shipping is judged relative to the product price, even within one industry.
Example: a $1,000 product with about $500 gross margin and shipping of up to $300 leaves **only about $200 for ads**.

Bringing shipping down to about $200 frees up enough money for ad costs and profit.
Targeting customers in states close to the supplier is one way to lower shipping.
Shipping costs vary widely by destination. Remote states such as Montana or Idaho can be far more expensive to ship to.
For a large item, a shipping cost of **$450 instead of $250** can push a product into the danger zone. The danger zone is where a product loses money or barely earns any.
Shipping costs depend on origin (where it ships from), destination, package size, weight

and the carrier (the shipping company) used.
You do not need exact numbers for every product at the start.
If shipping makes low-price items unprofitable, **sell only the higher-priced items** in that range.
Shipping can be quoted or estimated from the average shipping cost for each niche, when those averages are known.

Quotes are only needed when shipping costs are unknown.
Estimate shipping as follows.
1. **Ask your supplier** what it generally costs to ship an item from its location to your target regions.
2. Do not aim for exact figures. The cost varies per order unless the supplier offers flat-rate shipping, which is one fixed price per order.
3. Estimate a typical shipping cost for each product, and compare item A with item B.
4. **Enter the estimate** in the supplier shipping cost field and adjust it once real orders come in.
Shipping case and fix
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: Case: a seller had large, heavy products at about 9 x 57 x 36 inches and around 70 pounds.
The cheapest shipping found was **$198**. That covered FedEx, UPS and LTL. FedEx and UPS are parcel shipping companies. LTL means less-than-truckload, a freight service for large loads.
Profit before shipping was $150, so each sale lost about $50.
The advice was to ask the supplier how competitors ship at MAP. Ask for a better carrier or wholesale rate.
If competitors are losing money too, **either stop selling the item or raise the price** until it is profitable.

Procedure for a shipping cost that wipes out the margin on a product sold at MAP:
1. **Call the supplier** and state the exact shipping cost per unit and the loss per sale at MAP.
2. Tell the supplier which competitors sell the same product at MAP. Ask which carrier they use.
3. Ask whether the supplier can offer a better wholesale price or shipping rate.
4. If no competitor can sell profitably, **stop selling** the product or raise the price until each sale is profitable.
When rising shipping costs eat into margins, **ask suppliers** whether they offer a cheaper, slower shipping option. Ask about a shipping deal too.
Savings on shipping can protect margin before you raise retail prices.
**Add shipping costs** into the product cost used for pricing. Then the selling price already covers delivery.
Free shipping is only a sound offer if the supplier's alternative with free shipping is only a few dollars more expensive.
Express shipping can be offered as an **optional upgrade** for customers who want it.
Price setting without MAP
Procedure for suppliers without MAP
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t:
Procedure (undated):
1. **Apply for approval** with each supplier.
2. After approval, receive the supplier's price list.
3. Build your own price list. Add a third column for your sale price next to the wholesale cost and MSRP columns. MSRP means Manufacturer's Suggested Retail Price, the price the maker recommends.
4. **Set the sale price** using the 2x wholesale minimum. Go higher if competitors sell above that level.
5. **Review your paid advertising KPIs** every week. KPIs are key performance indicators, the numbers that show whether something works.

Structure of your own price list (supplier lists usually contain only the first two columns):
**Wholesale cost**: What you pay the supplier per unit (your cost of goods)
**MSRP**: Manufacturer's Suggested Retail Price, the selling price the manufacturer recommends
**Sale price**: Your own selling price, added by you because no MAP sets it outside MAP markets
For non-MAP suppliers, set a starting price of roughly **2.1 times** the wholesale cost.
p.h: Check the starting price against competitors

p.t:
Then compare with competitor prices on Google Shopping.
Competitors may be selling at 3 times MAP. That would make a higher price the right choice.

Check the supplier's listed MAP-free wholesale prices. MAP-free means no MAP applies.
Also check the prices two to three stores advertise for them.
1. Check the supplier's listed MAP-free wholesale prices and the prices two to three stores advertise them for.
2. If those stores sell at at least 2x wholesale, **list the product** at that price without undercutting them.
3. **Exclude these products** from your price match guarantee to avoid losses. A price match guarantee is a promise to match a rival's lower price.
Products of the same type can be offered by different companies at very different price levels. For example, about $700 from one company and about $3,500 from another.
A store that combines both price levels for a high-end supplier did not face pushback (complaints) from that supplier.
Raise margin without negotiating
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: Dropshipping means the supplier ships directly to your customer.
Dropshipping an accessory from the same manufacturer you already use solves the logistics side. Logistics means moving and shipping goods.
That makes **upsells and downsells** of existing brand accessories one of the easiest ways to raise margins in a store. An upsell offers a higher-priced item. A downsell offers a cheaper one.
Case: a dog toy was sourced for 6 USD from suppliers, while competitors sold it for 9.99 USD.
Competitors likely either bought in bulk or used slow AliExpress fulfillment. They accepted lower margins to win volume.
A beginner should **aim for higher margins** to reinvest profits, meaning put money back into the business.
So the choice was between raising the price or adding a shipping fee.
Negotiating better terms
Ask suppliers early about **volume-based pricing tiers** and incentive pricing.
Revisit negotiation when a product shows no margin, or when the store brings a large volume of sales to that supplier.

Once you have proven sales volume with a supplier, you can ask for better pricing terms.
If margins do not work from day one, **ask the supplier for better pricing** at the start.

A processing fee (a charge per order) of about $6 to $25 per order is uncommon.
It is acceptable when the order value is high, for example $200 to $300.

It can be negotiated later.
Template for volume-based pricing tiers:
Hi [Supplier name], We have just started selling your [brand or product line] on our website and want to grow this partnership.
Ask early and track volume (continued)

p.t: Do you have volume-based pricing tiers or discounts that unlock after a certain number of orders? Do you also have any incentive pricing we should know about for new retail partners?

Thank you, [Your name] [Company name]
Template for a margin-based request:

Hi [Supplier name], We have worked together for [time period] and we want the partnership to be profitable for both sides. Right now our profit margin on your products is only about [X]% after shipping.
We have seen competitors [Competitor A, B, C] selling the same products at [price] with free shipping. Are there better wholesale prices, better shipping rates or volume tiers we can access?
Could you also review our invoices for discounts we might be missing? We would like to make these products work for everyone. Thank you, [Your name] [Company name]
Template for a request on a product with too little margin:
Hi [CONTACT NAME], I was searching on Google and found [STORE 1], [STORE 2] and [STORE 3] selling [PRODUCT A], [PRODUCT B] and [PRODUCT C] at [COMPETITOR PRICE].
I checked our price list and our cost is [OUR COST] with shipping at [SHIPPING COST].
Is there any pricing incentive we could work on, such as a discount on the price list, a different tiered price list or better shipping rates?
We would love to promote these products and bring in sales, but there is simply not enough margin with our current price list. Could we set up a short call to go over this?

Thank you, [YOUR NAME], [COMPANY], [PHONE].
**Send it as written.** Then show the supplier the competitor prices you found and let them propose options.
Template for a product with negative net after shipping (negative net means you lose money after shipping; SKU means stock keeping unit, the product code) (2024):
Hi [Supplier contact name], we have recently been running our numbers. To run ads to your products profitably, we cannot sell at MAP and still keep a profit.
Is there any incentive or deal you could offer on the wholesale price for [product or SKU names]? Thank you, [Your name], [Store name].
Low-margin handling (continued)
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: Low-margin handling
A thin product is one with little margin left.
p.h: Decide what to do with a thin product

p.t:
Procedure when a supplier's margin is too low to fund ads (2023):
1. **Ask the supplier** if it has pricing incentives or different pricing tiers.
2. If nothing changes, list the products on the store without running ads for them and rely on organic traffic.

3. Only keep them if the margin is enough for the products to be worth the time.
Procedure when a product has negative net after shipping (2024):

1. **Ask the supplier** for a better wholesale price.
2. If the supplier says this is their best price, **exclude that product** from paid ads.
3. Add other suppliers who can offer better margins, so the budget goes to winning products.

Procedure when a supplier's product is priced below your margin needs (2021):
1. **Ask for better wholesale pricing** first.
2. If they refuse and the margin is too thin for ads, keep the product at MAP and rely on organic traffic without including it in Google Shopping, or **drop it**.
If a supplier gives a pricing incentive, the question is whether margins support ad spend. (2023)
If a supplier refuses any change in price structure, and competitors list at a **10 percent markup** over the supplier price, it is often not worth listing. (2023)
For a very poor supplier where little margin remains, either skip the products entirely or list them above MAP with no paid ads.
**Paid ads should be reserved** for products with enough margin to cover the ad cost.
Case: a seller had large, heavy products whose shipping cost wiped out the margin at MAP. The case and fix are in the shipping section above.
Ads or free traffic
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: If the remaining margin (the money you keep from a sale after costs) covers a sale at MAP (minimum advertised price,
the lowest price the brand lets you advertise) but not paid ads (ads you pay for), **exclude those products from Google Ads** and keep them listed.
Those products can still earn free Google product listing (a free product listing in Google Shopping) and organic traffic (free visitors who find you without ads).
Reserve paid ads for products with enough margin to cover the ad cost.
Before you run ads on a product, **confirm the target price covers the average cost per purchase** (the average ad cost to get one sale).
For TikTok ads, the source sets **3x landed cost** as the minimum sale price. Landed cost is the total cost to get the product to the customer, including product, shipping and fees.

Target product margin before running ads, so that sales are profitable and scalable (able to grow without losing money).
When the supplier's margin is too low, follow this order:

1. **Ask the supplier for incentives** (deals, discounts or better prices).
2. If that fails, **list the product without ads** and rely on organic traffic.
3. Keep the product only if the margin is worth the time.
If MAP enforcement (the brand's effort to make sellers follow MAP) fails after escalating up the supplier's chain of command (the order of managers you contact, from the rep upward),

**stop paid ads for that brand**.
Keep the products on the store for organic traffic only if the brand's MAP policy (its written pricing rules) allows it.
If a product has negative net after shipping (you lose money once shipping is paid) and the supplier cannot improve the price, **exclude it from paid ads**.
Move that budget to suppliers with better margins.
Before you pause ads on a product whose competitor is violating MAP, **search the competitor's name online and read the reviews**. (2023)
If reviews show poor customer service, late shipping or payment problems, the violator is likely to lose customers. In that case, it can be worth keeping ads running.
Direct-to-consumer means the brand sells straight to customers.
Undercutting means selling for less than others.
Supplier sales and temporary discounts can be listed on your store. **You do not need to worry about undercutting other suppliers.** (2023)
Direct-to-consumer undercutting and competitor prices (continued)
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t:
Contact brands around the holidays to ask if they will offer deals.
Your store can promote those discounts with graphics and emails.
Clearance items (old stock sold cheaply to clear it out) are typically exempt from MAP compliance.
So **a competitor selling clearance stock below MAP is not automatically a violation**.
If a supplier starts selling its best-selling products below your dealer cost (the price you pay the supplier) or discounts them heavily on its own site, **pause those products**.

Do not spend ad money on them until the supplier explains and corrects the pricing.
Some suppliers sell at a price so close to cost that a MAP violator cannot sustain it.
Such retailers tend to get bad reputations, so **check their reviews and customer complaints** before reacting to their price. (2023)
A retailer that sells below wholesale price (the price brands charge stores) is very likely a scam or burner store (a fake store that takes orders and money but never ships).
**Do not match such prices.** Build trust with your own store through reviews instead. (2024)
MAP violation monitoring and reporting
Testing whether a competitor violates MAP on Google Shopping (Google's price comparison page) (2023):

1. **Search the product on Google Shopping.**
2. Read the prices shown by the listings, including the free listings from three stores.
3. If most listings show one price and one or two show a much lower price, the most common price is probably MAP and the lower one is a violation.
**Search the brand name and SKU** (the product's stock code) in Google to find competitors selling below the minimum advertised price. (undated)

Copy the links to the competitor listings.
Expect manufacturers to use software to monitor MAP compliance.
Large retailers are less often penalized than smaller ones.
A distribution center (the supplier's warehouse) that warns you about not updating prices on time is a good sign. It means they care about you maximizing profit. (undated)
**Keep your product prices current** in your store to avoid these warnings.
Report the violation
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: When a supplier's MAP is known and a competitor sells below it, **report the violation to the supplier right away** with a screenshot. (2024)
Ask whether the competitor has a special deal. Ask whether the supplier will contact them.
Good suppliers enforce MAP and may remove an unauthorized retailer as an authorized dealer (a store officially approved by the brand).

Handling a MAP violation by a competitor (2021):
1. **Screenshot the competitor's product page** showing the low price.
2. Search the product in Google Shopping and screenshot the listing showing the same lower price.
3. **Email the supplier contact** with the competitor URL, both screenshots and a request to correct the pricing.

4. If the price is not updated within a few days, **reply to the same thread** (the same email conversation).
5. Most suppliers fix pricing quickly.

6. Amazon and Walmart listings below MAP can be reported to the supplier the same way.
Reporting procedure:
1. **Report every MAP violator to the supplier.**
2. Follow up with the supplier regularly.
3. If nothing changes after about one to two months, **stop selling that supplier's products** and stop spending ad budget on them.
4. Take screenshots of competitors selling below your cost, send them to the supplier, and ask whether a better pricing tier or incentive is available.
**Send the supplier screenshots** of the Google Shopping listing and the competitor's website.
A good supplier enforces MAP and responds within the number of days stated in the MAP policy.

If nothing changes, stop paid ads for that brand. Then either keep listings at MAP for organic traffic, or remove the supplier.
**Send the supplier links** to the competitor listings. (undated)
The supplier can then contact the violating retailer through its representatives.

p.t: Template for the first report:
Subject: MAP violation for [product name]. Hi [supplier contact name], we noticed that [competitor website] is currently selling [product name] for [price], which is below your MAP policy.
Here is the product page link: [competitor product URL]. I have attached a screenshot of the product page and a screenshot of the same listing in Google Shopping.

Could you please contact them and ask them to update their pricing? Thank you, [your name]
Template for the follow-up:
Subject: Follow-up on MAP violation for [product name]. Hi [supplier contact name], I am following up on my email from [date] about [competitor website] selling [product name] below MAP.

The price has not changed yet. Could you please check on this again? Thank you, [your name]
Template for asking about wholesale cost changes:
Subject: Question about wholesale costs. Hi [supplier contact name], I noticed on your website that [product 1] is listed at [price 1] and [product 2] at [price 2].
Is there an update to our wholesale costs that I should know about? I would appreciate a quick reply so I can plan my pricing. Thank you, [your name]
Template for a follow-up when a competitor is below MAP and the supplier has a special deal question (2024):
Hi [supplier contact name], thanks for sending the link to [competitor store URL]. I checked the site and it looks good.
I noticed that the MAP on [product name or SKU] is [MAP price], but they are listing it for [competitor listed price].
Could you let me know whether they have a special deal, or whether you will reach out to them to adjust their pricing? I have attached a screenshot for reference. Thank you, [your name]
Escalation and when to stop
p.s: Pricing, margin and profitability checks per supplier

p.t: If MAP enforcement fails after escalating up the supplier's chain of command, **stop paid ads for that brand**.

Keep the products on the store for organic traffic only if the MAP policy allows it.
Sources differ on timing.
The 2019 procedure stops selling after **about one to two months** without change.

The 2021 procedure responds to the number of days in the MAP policy, and then stops paid ads.
Use the timing in the supplier's MAP policy where it exists.
Where it does not exist, use the **one to two month** limit.
Not tracking exactly what you owe suppliers for each order leads to unexpected supplier bills (invoices).
Allocating a **COGS percentage** (the share of each sale that covers cost of goods sold, meaning what the products cost you) of every sale into a dedicated account gives a reserve that covers these
invoices.
Case: a high-ticket dropshipper (someone who sells expensive products that the supplier ships directly to the customer) had just started out.

Sales and profit were rising, and the owner believed the business was close to breaking even.
After several months, a supplier sent an unexpected bill of **10,000 to 15,000 dollars**.
The dropshipper had believed all supplier orders were paid, but they were not. The owner had to borrow money from friends and family to cover the bill.
**Allocate the COGS percentage** from into a dedicated account from each sale, so that supplier invoices are covered.
